subject: computing
subtitle: Linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and algorithm efficiency.

data.targetWord: a searching algorithm that checks each item in a list one by one from first to last until the target value is found or the entire list has been checked

examples.en-GB: A linear search for the value 7 in [3, 9, 7, 1, 5] checks index 0, then 1, then finds it at index 2 after 3 comparisons.

data.targetWord: a searching algorithm that repeatedly halves a sorted list by comparing the target to the middle element, eliminating the half that cannot contain the target

examples.en-GB: A binary search on [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20] for 14 finds it in just 3 comparisons by repeatedly halving the search space.

data.targetWord: a sorting algorithm that repeatedly compares adjacent pairs of elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order, until no swaps occur in a full pass

examples.en-GB: After the first pass of bubble sort on [5, 3, 8, 1, 4], the largest value 8 has bubbled up to its final position.

data.targetWord: a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that splits the list in half, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves back together; more efficient than bubble sort for large datasets

examples.en-GB: Merge sort splits [5, 3, 8, 1] into [5, 3] and [8, 1], sorts each half, then merges them into [1, 3, 5, 8].

data.targetWord: a sorting algorithm that builds a sorted list one element at a time by inserting each new element into its correct position in the already-sorted portion

examples.en-GB: Insertion sort takes each element in turn and slides it leftward past any larger elements until it is in the right place.

data.targetWord: checking whether one value is greater than, less than, or equal to another; the basic operation counted when measuring algorithm efficiency

examples.en-GB: In bubble sort, each comparison checks whether adjacent elements need to be swapped.

data.targetWord: one complete run through a list from start to end during a sorting algorithm, after which at least one more element is guaranteed to be in its final position

examples.en-GB: After the first pass of bubble sort, the largest element is always in its correct final position at the end of the list.

data.targetWord: the number of steps or comparisons an algorithm requires to complete its task; a more efficient algorithm requires fewer operations

examples.en-GB: Binary search is far more efficient than linear search: for 1,000 items it needs at most 10 comparisons versus up to 1,000.

data.targetWord: a list whose elements are arranged in ascending (lowest to highest) or descending order; required before binary search can be applied

examples.en-GB: The list [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20] is a sorted list in ascending order and is ready for binary search.

data.targetWord: exchanging the positions of two elements in a list, used in bubble sort when an adjacent pair is found to be in the wrong order

examples.en-GB: Comparing 5 and 3 in [5, 3, 8]: since 5 > 3, a swap produces [3, 5, 8].

data.targetWord: the middle element of a list (or sub-list) used in binary search to decide which half to search next

examples.en-GB: For the list [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20] the midpoint index is 3, giving the value 11.

data.targetWord: the numerical position of an element in a list, starting from 0 in most programming languages

examples.en-GB: In the list [3, 9, 7, 1, 5], the element 7 is at index 2.

data.targetWord: a finite, unambiguous set of steps designed to solve a problem; sorting and searching algorithms are fundamental examples

examples.en-GB: The bubble sort algorithm uses repeated passes and swaps to arrange a list in ascending order.

data.targetWord: one repetition of the main loop body in a searching or sorting algorithm, such as one comparison in a linear search or one pass in bubble sort

examples.en-GB: Each iteration of the linear search loop checks one element of the list against the target value.

data.targetWord: the maximum number of comparisons or steps an algorithm requires for any possible input, such as when the target is the last element or is absent

examples.en-GB: The worst case for linear search on a list of 10 items is 10 comparisons, when the target is the last element or not present.

data.targetWord: the minimum number of comparisons or steps an algorithm requires for any possible input, such as when the target is the first element checked

examples.en-GB: The best case for linear search is 1 comparison, when the target happens to be the very first element in the list.

data.targetWord: another name for linear search: checking items in order from first to last

examples.en-GB: A sequential search works on any list, sorted or unsorted, but can be slow for large datasets.

data.targetWord: a strategy used in binary search and merge sort where the problem is repeatedly split in half, reducing the amount of data to process at each step

examples.en-GB: Binary search uses divide and conquer: each comparison halves the remaining search space.

data.targetWord: a variable in binary search that tracks the lowest index of the current search region, starting at 0 and updated after each comparison

examples.en-GB: When the target is greater than the midpoint value, the low pointer is moved to midpoint + 1 to search the right half.

data.targetWord: a variable in binary search that tracks the highest index of the current search region, starting at the last index and updated after each comparison

examples.en-GB: When the target is less than the midpoint value, the high pointer is moved to midpoint - 1 to search the left half.

data.targetWord: two elements that are next to each other in a list; bubble sort compares and potentially swaps each adjacent pair in every pass

examples.en-GB: In [5, 3, 8], the adjacent pairs are (5, 3) and (3, 8); bubble sort compares each pair and swaps if out of order.

data.targetWord: the maximum number of passes bubble sort needs to fully sort a list of n elements in the worst case

examples.en-GB: A list of 5 elements needs at most 4 (n - 1) passes of bubble sort to be fully sorted.

data.targetWord: the core operation of binary search: splitting the remaining search space into two equal halves and discarding the half that cannot contain the target

examples.en-GB: Binary search's halving strategy means a sorted list of 1,000 items requires at most 10 comparisons to find any value.

data.targetWord: an arrangement of list elements from lowest to highest value; the standard order required for binary search

examples.en-GB: [1, 3, 5, 8, 12] is in ascending order and can be searched efficiently with binary search.

data.targetWord: the result returned by a searching algorithm when the target value is absent from the list, typically indicated by returning -1

examples.en-GB: If the target is not in the list, linear search checks every element and returns -1 to indicate not found.

data.title: Steps in binary search
data.instruction: Put the steps of binary search in the correct order.
items: Set low = first index, high = last index
Compare target to the element at midpoint
If match: return the midpoint index
If target is less: set high = midpoint - 1
If target is greater: set low = midpoint + 1
Repeat from step 2 until found or low > high

data.instruction: Put these comparisons and swaps in the correct order for the first pass of bubble sort on [5, 3, 8, 1].
items: End of pass 1: 8 is now in its final position

data.title: Steps in linear search
data.instruction: Put the steps of linear search in the correct order.
items: Start at the first item in the list (index 0)
Compare the current item to the target value
If they match: return the current index
If they do not match: move to the next item
Repeat the comparison for the next item
If the end of the list is reached without a match: return -1
